meta.title: Who really said "Hate destroys the hater"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: A folk proverb documented since 1897, not an MLK original. King preached a fuller version in 1957: “hate destroys the hater as well as the hated.”
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Hate destroys the hater'?
meta.ogDescription: Not an MLK original. This is an anonymous proverb attested since 1897. King preached a longer version in his 1957 “Loving Your Enemies” sermon.

answer.label: Not original to Martin Luther King Jr. — an older anonymous proverb
answer.authorDates: Proverb in circulation by 1897 · popularized in the U.S. through the 20th century
answer.sourceLine: The compact line “Hate destroys the hater” is a folk proverb that Quote Investigator traces to at least 1897 ↗ and whose originator it designates as anonymous. King did express the idea — in his 1957 sermon “Loving Your Enemies” he said “hate destroys the hater as well as the hated” — but he neither coined the saying nor used this exact three-word wording.

source.heading: Where it actually comes from

docMeta.dd: “Loving Your Enemies,” Dexter Avenue Baptist Church, 17 Nov 1957

source.excerpt: Hate at any point is a cancer that gnaws away at the very vital center of your life and your existence. It is like eroding acid that eats away the best and the objective center of your life. So Jesus says love, because hate destroys the hater as well as the hated.
trail: 1897: Henry Norman’s book Real already frames the idea — “the nature of hatred is to first destroy the hated one and then destroy the hater” — and a July 1897 theosophy journal adds “it is a poison and destroys the hater,” per Quote Investigator ↗.

1916–1921: American speakers and papers sharpen it — Louis N. Whealton (1916): “Hate at last destroys the hater”; Peter Witt (1921): “Hate can’t injure the person hated. But it destroys the hater” (QI ↗).

1957: Martin Luther King Jr. preaches “hate destroys the hater as well as the hated” in “Loving Your Enemies” ↗ — a genuine King line, but a later and fuller instance of a decades-old proverb, not its origin.
Verdict: Quote Investigator designates the proverb’s originator as anonymous ↗; the bare three-word form is a modern compression pinned onto famous names.
source.excerptNote: Martin Luther King Jr.’s actual wording in the 1957 “Loving Your Enemies” sermon — the fuller thought from which the compressed proverb is often quoted in his name.

sourceLink.text: Quote Investigator: Hate Ultimately Destroys the Hater

source.rightsNote: The compressed line “Hate destroys the hater” has no single identifiable author — it is a folk proverb attested in varying wordings since 1897, so no clean public-domain claim attaches to this exact three-word form. King’s own fuller wording is from a 1957 sermon and would be in-copyright to the King estate; the anonymous proverb it echoes predates 1931 in its earliest attestations.

author.name: Martin Luther King Jr.
author.heading: Who King was — and what he actually said
author.bio: Martin Luther King Jr. (1929–1968) led the American civil-rights movement and, as pastor of Dexter Avenue Baptist Church in Montgomery, built much of his ethic of nonviolence around the destructive power of hatred. In his 1957 sermon Loving Your Enemies he preached that “hate destroys the hater as well as the hated” — a genuine King line. But the bare proverb “Hate destroys the hater” predates him by decades and belongs to no single author.

cite.sourceCitation: Earliest documented in Henry Norman, Real (1897) and A. P. Buchman, The Theosophical Forum (July 1897); King’s fuller wording in Martin Luther King Jr., “Loving Your Enemies,” sermon delivered at Dexter Avenue Baptist Church, Montgomery, Ala., 17 November 1957. Provenance per Quote Investigator (2020).

misattribution.heading: How it gets misattributed
misattribution.intro: The tidy three-word line is a magnet for famous names. In reality it is an anonymous proverb whose wording drifted for over a century; the figures below each used a version of it, but none originated the compact form.

items.why: King really did preach “hate destroys the hater as well as the hated” in 1957, so quote sites shorten it to “Hate destroys the hater” and stamp his name on it — but the proverb was already in print in 1897, decades before King was born ↗.

The Carver version — “hate within will ultimately destroy the hater” — rests entirely on Alvin D. Smith’s 1954 memoir recalling Carver’s 1915–1919 Bible classes, with no earlier primary source from Carver himself ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: The saying belongs to no one famous: Quote Investigator concludes the proverb’s originator is anonymous ↗, evolving through many voices from 1897 onward.

context.heading: Why it matters
lead: The line survives because it compresses a moral intuition — that hatred corrodes the one who holds it — into three words. That very compression is what lets it float free of any real source and attach to whichever admired figure a reader trusts most.

King’s authentic teaching on this theme is richer than the slogan: in Loving Your Enemies he called hate “a cancer that gnaws away at the very vital center of your life,” and in Strength to Love (1963) he wrote that “like an unchecked cancer, hate corrodes the personality.” Crediting him with the bare proverb flattens that into a bumper sticker.
context.pull: A genuine King idea — but a proverb older than King himself.
